t: Divisor Game — Game Theory Meets a One-Line Insight
o: Two players alternately pick a divisor x of the current n (with 0 < x < n) and replace n with n - x; whoever cannot move loses. Alice moves first, and we must decide whether she wins with optimal play. For n = 2, Alice picks x = 1, leaving Bob with 1, so Bob cannot move — Alice wins. For n = 3, Alice is forced to pick x = 1, leaving 2 to Bob, who then leaves 1 to Alice, who loses. The constraint n <= 1000 means even an O(n^2) DP over all states is trivially fast, but the structure of the game hides a constant-time pattern.
k: A position is winning if any move leads to a losing position for the opponent, and losing if all moves lead to winning positions.
Every move subtracts at least 1, so parity of n changes each turn; only odd numbers can be left as losing states.
Alice wins if and only if n is even: from an even n she can always play x = 1 (handing Bob an odd number), while from odd n every divisor is odd, forcing her to hand Bob an even number.

a.i: Define win[k] as whether the player about to move with number k wins. By standard impartial-game analysis, win[k] is true iff there exists a divisor x of k such that win[k - x] is false. We compute this bottom-up from win[1] = false.
s: Create a boolean array dp of size n + 1, with dp[1] = false (no moves available).
For each k from 2 to n, iterate over all divisors x < k (x from 1 to k/2).
Set dp[k] = true if any dp[k - x] is false; otherwise it stays false.
a.t: O(n^2) in the worst case — for each state k we scan up to k/2 candidate divisors.

a.i: Claim: the current player wins exactly when n is even. If n is odd, all its divisors are odd, so n - x is even — you must hand your opponent an even number. If n is even, playing x = 1 hands the opponent an odd number. Since 1 is a terminal loss, by induction every even n is a win and every odd n is a loss for the player to move. Alice starts, so she wins iff n is even.
s: Base case: n = 1 is a loss (odd), n = 2 is a win (even).
Inductive step: from odd n, every legal move yields an even number, which is a winning state for the opponent.
From even n, choose x = 1, yielding odd n - 1, a losing state for the opponent.

w: In an interview, start with the memoized DP to demonstrate correct game-theory reasoning, then derive the O(1) parity solution as the punchline — mentioning both shows depth. Common pitfalls: forgetting that x must be a proper divisor (x < n), assuming Alice should always pick the largest divisor (she shouldn't — picking 1 suffices from even n), and mishandling n = 1 (Alice loses immediately). Edge cases are just n = 1 (false) and n = 2 (true). Likely follow-ups: generalize to 'subtract any divisor' variants, count optimal first moves, or analyze the game where players may add instead of subtract.
